notes: Traced every cited path; the finding is accurate. config.json and jobs.json both use raw File.WriteAllText after a best-effort .bak copy, and the corrupt-load recovery (TryBackupCorrupt copies, never moves; .bak never consulted) means the very next Save — guaranteed within seconds by the startup update check writing LastCheckTime (CheckOnStartup defaults true), or at latest on app close — copies the still-corrupt file over the only good backup. The scheduler concurrency claims also hold (jobStorage.Save on ThreadPool timer threads, no lock, UI enumerates Jobs.Values on a 5s timer; the false "crashed during execution" report follows from a throwing CompleteJob save). Only minor nuance: the dictionary mid-enumeration race needs a UI-thread job add/delete (scheduler saves only overwrite existing keys), but the cross-thread unsynchronized access and File.WriteAllText collision are real regardless. Critical severity is justified: one torn write during routine automatic saves permanently destroys all presets, environments, and job definitions despite a good backup existing moments earlier. | impact check: Traced every citation; the finding holds as written. The decisive part is verified end-to-end: after a corrupt load, TryBackupCorrupt COPIES (leaves the corrupt config.json in place), .bak is never consulted, and the very next Save — guaranteed within seconds by the unconditional LastCheckTime write after the startup update check (CheckOnStartup defaults true), or at app close — copies the corrupt file over the last-good .bak before writing defaults. So a single torn write becomes permanent loss of all presets/environments/jobs despite WriteJsonAtomic existing and being used by the sibling history services; the recommendation is sound and not implemented anywhere for these two files. One minor nuance: the scheduler's jobs-dictionary writes are existing-key overwrites, which on .NET 8 don't invalidate enumerators, so the "mutate mid-enumeration" crash is less likely in practice than implied (the concurrent File.WriteAllText IOException and false 'crashed during execution' report are real, MaxConcurrentJobs defaults to 3). Critical is justified per rubric: unrecoverable data loss with constant exposure (config saves on every settings change/close; jobs.json rewritten twice per scheduled run).

Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: TryGetPassword blocks the WinForms UI thread on GetAwaiter().GetResult() (VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49), VaultService has zero ConfigureAwait(false) (verified by grep), and ExecutePresetOnRowsAsync reaches GetHostConnections/TryGetPassword with no prior await from async-void UI handlers — so any uncached vault_path read (first run after launch, post-300s-TTL, new path/profile) posts its HTTP continuation to the blocked UI thread: permanent hang, force-kill required. Only nit: the OIDC aside is slightly off — an expired OIDC token deadlocks at the first auth_url HTTP await before the browser/HttpListener flow ever launches (same hang, not worse). The same blocking call is also reachable from the parallel connection-test path (Form1.cs:8916). Critical severity is justified: app-wide hang on the primary Run path for Vault-backed hosts. | impact check: Traced end-to-end and it holds: TryGetPassword blocks on GetResult (VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49), VaultService.cs has zero ConfigureAwait(false), and all five run entry points are async-void UI handlers reaching GetHostConnections().ToList() (Form1.cs:12277) with no prior await — so the first uncached vault read posts its HTTP continuation to the blocked UI thread: permanent deadlock, and HttpClient's timeout cannot rescue it (the fault continuation also needs the UI thread). Only nit: the OIDC parenthetical is slightly off — it deadlocks at the first HTTP continuation before any browser launches — and note ConfigureAwait(false) alone removes the deadlock but still freezes the UI for the HTTP duration, so the async-off-UI-thread option is the real fix.

Traced end-to-end and the claim holds exactly as written. In json+append mode, any merge failure (unparseable existing file, non-object appended onto an object file, read exception, or even a scalar JSON root) makes MergeJsonContent return null, FormatAsJson falls through to serializing only the new value, and ExecuteAsync's File.WriteAllText(:101) replaces the whole file — then returns CommandResult.Ok(). The "silent" part is stronger than the finding states: ScriptContext.EmitOutput (ScriptContext.cs:875) drops ALL Debug-level output unless DebugMode is on, so in a normal run there is zero visible trace. All writes are non-atomic, so the command can manufacture its own corrupt file that triggers the wipe on the next run. Cited line numbers are accurate; the recommended fixes (fail the step, .bak the file, atomic write) are not implemented anywhere in the command. | impact check: Traced and confirmed: every merge-failure path in FormatAsJson (parse error :283-285, non-object-into-object :276-277, read exception :229-232) falls through to serializing only the new value, which File.WriteAllText at :101 then writes over the entire file — with Debug-only diagnostics and a successful step result, so on_error never fires. No mitigating layer exists: no .bak, writes are non-atomic, JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic is unused here, and tests cover only JSONL/text append (the fall-through is not a tested contract). SCRIPTING.md (:2105, :5189, :6323) actively recommends the multi-host JSON-append accumulator pattern and documents only "intelligent merging", never the silent-overwrite fallback. One nuance: with the documented array-accumulator pattern a malformed NEW value is harmlessly appended as a string — total loss requires the existing file to be unparseable (torn write, hand edit, concurrent writer) or an object-file/non-object mismatch — but the command's own non-atomic writes can create exactly that torn file, and the loss is silent and unrecoverable, so critical stands.

The headline claim is wrong for the common scalar form: ScriptParser.ParseExitStep normalizes shorthand exits before execution, prepending a literal "success " to any bare message (ScriptParser.cs:1469, deliberate per its comment), so `exit: "{{summary}}"` becomes "success {{summary}}" and runtime data can never flip the status; `exit: "Could not reach host"` exits Success by design, not via the cited ExitCommand fall-through (which is unreachable for scalar exits). A narrower real bug remains in the mapping form: `exit: { message: "{{x}}" }` without status: leaves step.Exit as the bare message (ScriptParser.cs:1432-1435), where ExitCommand's substitute-then-parse (ExitCommand.cs:18, 24-64) does derive status from runtime data or silently defaults to Success; also the mapping's status: value is never validated (ScriptParser.cs:1413), so `status: failed` silently exits Success. Worth fixing, but the trigger is much narrower than claimed — medium, not high.

notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: ReleaseSession (SshConnectionPool.cs:272-280) unconditionally removes the single per-key lease, and both callers' finally blocks (SshExecutionService.cs:1570, 2154) release even when they were standalone (non-lease-owning) callers, so a finishing preset clears the active holder's lease and a later same-key CreateSessionAsync re-leases the pooled Ssh client the holder is still driving; standalone clients from the collision path (SshConnectionPool.cs:251) are never tracked, never disposed by SshShellSession.Dispose (1446-1474) or by callers, and the cleanup sweep only iterates _connections, so each collision leaks a live SSH connection. notes: The symptom is real — a typo'd function in an iif condition silently yields a constant branch instead of an error — but the described mechanism is wrong. For the cited example `iif(lenght(x) > 0, ...)`, the FormatException from ExpressionParser.cs:436 is caught INSIDE ExpressionEvaluator.ResolveValue (lines 331-340), never reaching Iif's bare catch; ResolveNumeric then coerces "lenght(x)" to 0, so 0 > 0 = false and the ELSE branch is pinned (not the then-branch as claimed). The then-branch is only pinned for operator-less conditions like `iif(lenght(x), a, b)`, again via Evaluate's own truthy fallback, not Iif's catch (which is nearly unreachable — built-in function handlers are defensive). Consequently the recommended fix in MathFunctions.Iif would not change the typo behavior; the silent fallback to fix is in ExpressionEvaluator.ResolveValue/ResolveNumeric, which also affects if:/while: conditions.

The missing guards are real (no IsHandleCreated check, unguarded BeginInvoke lambda, threadpool event delivery all verified at the cited lines), but both headline failure modes don't hold. (1) Scintilla5.NET forces handle creation on any property access, and the control's own constructor (ApplyTheme, line 210) creates the inner editor's handle on the UI thread before validation can ever be requested — so a pre-handle delivery cannot create the handle on a threadpool thread or "permanently break" the control; the residual risk is a cross-thread direct native call, and the window closes at JobEditorDialog.cs:230 (SetDarkTitleBar forces the form handle ~8 lines after the text assignment), making the >=150-400ms debounced result landing inside it extremely unlikely. (2) The disposal race is neutralized in practice: control Dispose unsubscribes the handler (2588-2591), JobEditorDialog disposes the validation service (cancelling pending work) before the editor (2149-2150), WinForms abandons pending BeginInvoke callbacks on handle destruction (never executed), and the worst-case ObjectDisposedException lands in the fire-and-forget validation task and is swallowed unobserved — no crash. The recommended hardening is still worthwhile defensive hygiene, but this is polish, not a realistic crash window.
